title: Six examples, one bad lesson
spec: M07 · selection, ordering, and the knee
intro: A debtor extractor with six few-shot examples scores 73%. Four examples score 96% and cost less. In between sits one demonstration that taught the model to name the lender as the debtor — and a curve that goes flat at four.

provenance.source: a narrated few-shot eval over a 200-filing UCC test set; accuracies, token counts and prices are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: The block this walks is M07's A Diverse Few-Shot Block for UCC Extraction — four examples spanning null, cross-reference, flagging and the happy path, canonical last.

steps.title: Six examples, and it still invents debtors
narrative: The extractor pulls the debtor name out of a UCC filing and returns JSON. Its system prompt says, in plain prose, return null when the debtor is redacted. Underneath that sentence sit six worked examples: five clean UCC-1 filings and one hard case.

On a 200-filing eval set it scores 73%. Split by input class the number stops being a single fact and becomes a diagnosis: 97.9% on clean filings and 4% on redacted ones. The rule is right there in the prose. The examples outvoted it.
steps.youDo: Grade your own few-shot block per input class, not in aggregate. An 80% that hides a 4% class is the only number that matters and the one an aggregate score erases.

steps.title: The example that taught the wrong lesson
narrative: Example six was supposed to be the hard case. The curator went looking for a redacted filing, found 2019-FL-0007740 — redacted debtor, but with a D/B/A NORTHBAY MARINE SUPPLY line two rows down — and wrote the expected output as {"debtor_name": "NORTHBAY MARINE SUPPLY"}, because a human reading that page can obviously recover the name.

It is a correct label on an unrepresentative input. One filing in the corpus carries a d/b/a line under a redaction; the other twenty-three do not. So the demonstration does not teach use the d/b/a line when there is one — there is no second example to bound it. It teaches when the name is hidden, keep looking until you find one.

The model obeys. On 2024-FL-0021077 the debtor is redacted and there is no d/b/a line, so it takes the next capitalised entity on the page — the secured party. The extractor reports the lender as the debtor, with an empty flags array and no hedging anywhere.
steps.claudeSays: Nothing in the six examples shows me returning null. The one example about a hidden name shows me recovering it. I generalised the only pattern I was given.

expected {"debtor_name": null, "flags": ["redacted"]}  — the LENDER was reported as the DEBTOR
⛔ 23 of 24 redacted filings produced a fabricated debtor, none flagged

after.title: AFTER — what the model actually generalised

views.text: One example cannot teach an exception; with nothing to bound it, it teaches a rule. The demonstrated rule here is "a debtor name is always recoverable" — and the model applies it to the 23 filings where it is false.

steps.title: Four examples that match the distribution
narrative: Throw the block away and select against the real input distribution instead of against how a hard case felt. Four examples: a redacted filing mapping to null, a UCC-3 amendment mapping to see_original, an 80-character name carrying possibly_truncated, and the clean canonical case last so its format is the most recent thing the model saw.

Accuracy goes from 73.0% to 96.0% and the block gets smaller — 610 tokens down to 400. Redacted filings go from 1/24 to 23/24, because for the first time the model has seen null come out of the extractor.
Note what did not change: the prose rules are byte-identical. The 23-point move is entirely a selection decision.
steps.youDo: Count your real input classes first, then pick one example per class. If a class has no example, the model has never seen the behaviour you want on it.

terminal.text:
- 5 clean UCC-1 examples, 1 d/b/a recovery example       610 tokens
+ redacted -> null, amendment -> see_original,
+ 80-char -> possibly_truncated, clean canonical LAST    400 tokens

steps.title: Where the curve goes flat
narrative: Four worked. So does five buy more? Keep adding diverse examples to the same block and grade each one. Examples one through four move accuracy 71% → 96%. Examples five through eight move it 96% → 96%, with a 0.5-point bump at six that is one filing out of two hundred and comes back off at eight.

Those four extra examples cost 430 tokens on every call. At 40,000 extractions a day and $3 per million input tokens that is 17.2M tokens and $51.60 a day for zero points. The six-example variant buys its half-point — one filing in two hundred — for $25.20 a day, which a compliance pipeline might genuinely want and a bulk indexer never would.

One more knob, and it is free: move the clean canonical example from last position to third and the same four examples score 95.0% instead of 96.0%. Recency anchors the output format. Ordering is worth a point and costs nothing.
steps.youDo: Run your own block at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8 examples and plot it. The knee is a measurement, not a rule of thumb, and it moves with the task.

terminal.text: stop rule: k=4 (first k within 0.5 pts of the max, cheapest)

cells: −1.0 pt for free — ordering, not count

view.text: Examples one to four bought coverage of the input classes; five to eight bought tokens. Select one demonstration per real input class, put the canonical format last, measure the knee, and stop there — and treat every example as a claim about the distribution, because an unrepresentative one does not add a little noise, it teaches a rule the model will apply everywhere.
